title: Where engineering judgment fits in AI-assisted development
summary: AI can speed up implementation and investigation. Deciding whether the result fits a production system still takes context, review, and experience.
bodyHtml:
The more I work with AI coding tools, the more useful I find them for exploring an unfamiliar problem, investigating a defect, and getting an initial implementation in place. They give me more options to examine and a shorter feedback loop.

They also make it easier to produce a convincing answer before the underlying question is settled. That changes how I spend my attention during development.

Supply the context that changes the answer

A tool can work from the requirements and code available to it. The engineer still needs to identify missing business rules, operational constraints, and dependencies. A clean implementation may solve only part of the problem if those details never enter the conversation.

Check the decisions behind the code

I want to understand why a change uses a particular boundary, where its data comes from, and how it behaves when a dependency fails. Reading the output is one part of that review; tracing the behavior through the existing application is another.

Experience helps me decide which questions deserve more investigation. It does not make review optional. An unfamiliar library or a subtle assumption is a reason to check further.

Keep understanding close to delivery

I see AI as a useful part of the development process, alongside direct investigation, discussion, and verification. The measure of success is software I can explain and maintain after the initial change is complete.

Faster implementation gives engineering judgment more work to do. I want to use that time to improve the decisions around the code as well as the code itself.
